title: What is the PwC and Strategy& interview process, and how should you prepare?
description: How PwC consulting and its strategy arm Strategy& hire: CV screening, online tests, candidate-led cases, group cases and presentations.
hook: PwC's consulting roles and its strategy arm, Strategy&, recruit separately: PwC's early-careers route runs through online tests, a video interview and assessment stages, while Strategy& runs a case-heavy process much closer to MBB. Both vary by country and role. Here is what each looks like, with the details PwC and Strategy& publish, and how to prepare.
body:
PwC consulting and Strategy&

Strategy& is PwC's strategy consulting business. It was Booz & Company until PwC completed its acquisition in April 2014 and renamed it. It recruits separately from the rest of PwC and focuses on strategy problems, while PwC's wider consulting business covers technology, operations, deals, risk and transformation work.

So the first question is which one you are applying to. The interview, and the preparation, differ.

The PwC UK early-careers process

PwC UK publishes its selection process for students and graduates. As of 2026 it runs:

  1. Online application.
  2. Online assessment on the SHL platform: an untimed behavioural profile and a timed cognitive test covering numerical, inductive and deductive reasoning.
  3. On-demand video interview: recorded answers about your experience, reviewed later by an assessor.
  4. Virtual assessment centre.
  5. Business assessment: for graduate programmes, after you are matched to a business area and office, a final in-person interview with a senior leader from that area.
  6. Offer.

Other countries and experienced-hire routes differ, and consulting roles may include case interviews, so check your invitation.

The Strategy& process: an example

Strategy&'s Amsterdam office publishes an unusually detailed process, which gives a good picture of what to expect:

  1. Apply online with your CV, transcripts and a cover letter.
  2. Online assessment of about 60 minutes, with a cognitive and a behavioural part. A practice test is available.
  3. Preparation: a recruiter schedules your interviews, and you get a practice case with a consultant and a "buddy" for guidance.
  4. First round: three 60-minute interviews with consultants, mixing personal fit and case questions.
  5. Second round: three similar interviews with senior colleagues.
  6. Feedback and offer.

The office says cases are usually based on real client work and take about half of each interview. You are asked to structure and work through an open business problem using hypotheses, and interviewers focus on your approach and thinking rather than the final answer. Other offices vary, but this shape, several case interviews across two rounds, is typical of strategy firms.

What the cases test

Strategy& cases are generally candidate-led, similar in style to BCG and Bain: you clarify, structure, ask for data, do the maths and recommend. Practise driving the case and working from a hypothesis. Some processes also include a group exercise or a presentation prepared alone.

A worked example: should a payments company lend?

Prompt: A payments company wants to enter small-business lending. Is it worth it? (Illustrative numbers.)

A strategy structure covers the size and profitability of the opportunity, target customer segments, competitors, credit losses, funding costs, regulation and whether the client has an advantage, such as data on its merchants' sales. A technology-delivery interview for PwC consulting might focus instead on underwriting workflows, data quality, platform integration and controls. Both are real consulting problems; the emphasis differs.

Now the economics. The company plans a $200M loan book earning an 8% yield, funded at 4%, with expected credit losses of 2% a year.

  • Interest income: $200M × 8% = $16M.
  • Funding cost: $200M × 4% = $8M.
  • Credit losses: $200M × 2% = $4M.
  • Spread after losses: $16M − $8M − $4M = $4M a year, before operating costs and the cost of holding capital.

If running the lending business costs $2.5M a year, profit falls to $1.5M. The candidate who calls the 8% "revenue" and stops there has missed the economics of lending.

Weak: "The loans earn 8%, so $16M a year. That looks attractive."
Strong: "After funding and expected losses, the book makes about $4M, and roughly $1.5M after operating costs. The answer hinges on credit losses: each extra point costs $2M. The company's merchant sales data could help it underwrite better than banks, so I'd test that in a pilot with existing merchants."

How to prepare

  • For Strategy&: practise candidate-led cases, including at least one presentation-style case you prepare alone and then present. Read up on how banks make money if financial services cases are likely.
  • For PwC consulting: practise timed reasoning tests, recorded video answers and competency stories, then cases if your role includes them.
  • For both: prepare clear answers to why PwC or why Strategy&, naming the kind of work you want; one story about your analytical contribution; and one about influencing people without authority.
  • If your process includes a group exercise, practise contributing without dominating.

Processes and practice names change across countries and roles. Treat published examples and candidate reports as a guide, and confirm your format with your recruiter.

Practice

In the lending case, expected credit losses turn out to be 3%, not 2%. What is the spread after losses, and does the business still make money after $2.5M of operating costs?

Show the answer

Losses: $200M × 3% = $6M. Spread: $16M − $8M − $6M = $2M. After $2.5M of operating costs, the business loses $0.5M a year. One point of credit losses turns a profit into a loss, which is why underwriting quality is the heart of the case.

Where to go next

Compare with Deloitte and EY-Parthenon, and if a group exercise is on your schedule, read how group and written cases work.
